sources.quote: את המנרה הטהרה על שם שלא היה מזין עליה שום דם
sources.says: Chizkuni says it is called pure because no blood was sprinkled on it.

sources.quote: לא היה שם כלי כולו של זהב שלא היה בו עץ חוץ מן המנורה
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says no vessel there was all gold without wood except the menorah.

39:11.headline: נפך: Judah's stone, which makes enemies turn their backs
39:11.body: Rabbeinu Bahya says the נפך was Judah's stone. Whoever wears it, he says, sees his enemies turn their backs, הופכין, and that is why it is called נפך, as Jacob blessed Judah: 'your hand on your enemies' neck'.

sources.quote: וסגולת האבן הזאת שכל מי שנושאם אויביו הופכין לו עורף ולכך נקרא נפך
sources.says: Bahya says whoever carries this stone sees his enemies turn their backs, and so it is called נפך.

39:12.headline: אחלמה: Gad's stone, named for strength
39:12.body: Rabbeinu Bahya says the אחלמה was Gad's stone. It strengthens the heart so a man does not lose courage in war, and it is named from חלם, 'strong', as in Hezekiah's 'You made me strong and gave me life'.

sources.quote: וסגולת האבן הזאת שמחזקת את הלב שלא ירך בלכתו למלחמה ולכך נקראת אחלמה מלשון חוזק
sources.says: Bahya says this stone strengthens the heart so one does not weaken going to war, so it is named אחלמה, from strength.

39:13.headline: ישפה, Benjamin's stone: 'there is a mouth', yet he kept silent
39:13.body: Rabbeinu Bahya reads ישפה as two words, יש פה, 'there is a mouth'. Benjamin wrestled over whether to tell his father about Joseph's sale, and he held his tongue.

sources.quote: ונקראת ישפה שתי מלות יש פה, וזה יורה על מעלתו שאע"פ שהיה לו פה והיה לו לגלות הדבר שתק ולא גלה
sources.says: Bahya says ישפה is two words, יש פה: though Benjamin had a mouth and could have revealed the matter, he kept silent.

8:2.headline: 'The frog came up': one frog, or a whole swarm?
8:2.body: The verse says הצפרדע, 'the frog', in the singular. Rashi cites a midrash that there was one frog which spewed out swarms each time it was struck, and also gives the plain sense: a swarm is spoken of as one.

sources.quote: צְפַרֵדַּע אַחַת הָיְתָה וְהָיוּ מַכִּין אוֹתָהּ וְהִיא מַתֶּזֶת נְחִילִים נְחִילִים, זֶהוּ מִדְרָשׁוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the midrash is that there was one frog; they struck it and it spurted out swarm after swarm.

sources.quote: וּפְשׁוּטוֹ יֵשׁ לוֹמַר, שֵׁרוּץ הַצְפַרְדְּעִים קוֹרֵא לְשׁוֹן יְחִידוּת
sources.says: Rashi says the plain meaning is that the swarm of frogs is called by a singular word.

8:5.headline: 'Glorify yourself over me': Moses dares Pharaoh to set a hard test
8:5.body: Rashi reads התפאר עלי as 'boast over me', like an axe boasting over the one who chops with it: name a hard task and say I cannot do it. Ibn Ezra reads it the other way: I will give you the honor of choosing the day.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ "הֲיִתְפָּאֵר הַגַּרְזֶן עַל הַחֹצֵב בּוֹ" (ישעיהו י
sources.says: Rashi compares 'shall the axe boast over the one who hews with it' (Isaiah 10).

sources.quote: וְכֵן הִתְפָּאֵר עָלַי – הִשְׁתַּבֵּחַ לְהִתְחַכֵּם וְלִשְׁאֹל דָּבָר גָּדוֹל, וְלוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא אוּכַל לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says Moses means: boast and be clever, ask for something great and say I will not be able to do it.

sources.quote: אעשה לך תפארת שאעתיר אל השם ויסר המכה ביום שתבקש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Moses means: I will do you honor, for I will pray to God and the plague will leave on the day you ask.

8:6.headline: Why Pharaoh asked for tomorrow instead of right now
8:6.body: Anyone would want a plague to end at once. Ibn Ezra cites Rav Shmuel ben Chofni: Pharaoh thought the stars had brought the frogs and Moses knew they were about to leave anyway, so he asked for tomorrow to test him.

sources.quote: אין מנהג האדם לבקש רק שיסור המכה ממנו מיד, וחשב פרעה כי מערכת כוכבי השמים הביאה הצפרדעים על מצרים, ומשה הוא יודע זה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra, citing Rav Shmuel ben Chofni, says people normally ask for a plague to end at once, but Pharaoh thought the arrangement of the stars brought the frogs and that Moses knew this.

sources.quote: על כן נסהו להאריך ואמר למחר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Pharaoh therefore tested him by delaying, and said 'tomorrow'.

8:12.headline: Moses does not strike the dust that once hid his secret
8:12.body: God tells Aaron, not Moses, to strike the dust. Rashi says the dust had protected Moses when he buried the Egyptian he killed in the sand, so it was not fitting for Moses to strike it.

sources.quote: לֹא הָיָה הֶעָפָר כְּדַאי לִלְקוֹת עַ"יְ מֹשֶׁה, לְפִי שֶׁהֵגֵן עָלָיו כְּשֶׁהָרַג אֶת הַמִּצְרִי וַיִּטְמְנֵהוּ בַּחוֹל, וְלָקָה עַל יְדֵי אַהֲרֹן
sources.says: Rashi says the dust did not deserve to be struck by Moses, since it protected him when he killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand, so it was struck by Aaron.

8:15.headline: The magicians' name loses a letter when their power fails
8:15.body: Until now the Torah spells חרטמים, magicians, with a י. Bahya notes that here, when they fail, it is spelled החרטמם without the י, because their wisdom fell short.

sources.quote: עד עתה הזכיר החרטמים מלא ביו"ד אבל במכה זו של כנים שהזכיר בה ולא יכלו הזכיר החרטמם חסר יו"ד כי בכאן חסרה חכמתם וכשל כחם
sources.says: Bahya says until now it wrote 'magicians' with a yod, but in the plague of lice, where it says they could not, it writes it without the yod, because here their wisdom was lacking and their power failed.

8:15.headline: 'The finger of God': a confession, or a shrug at the stars?
8:15.body: Rashi reads it as the magicians admitting this plague came from God, not sorcery. Ibn Ezra says they chose the general word אלהים, not God's name, to say it came from the stars over Egypt and not for Israel's sake, which is why Pharaoh stayed hard.

sources.quote: מַכָּה זוֹ אֵינָהּ עַל יְדֵי כְשָׁפִים, מֵאֵת הַמָּקוֹם הִיא
sources.says: Rashi says this plague is not by sorcery; it is from God.

sources.quote: לא באה זאת המכה בעבור ישראל לשלחם, רק מכת אלהים היא כפי מערכת הכוכבים על מזל ארץ מצרים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they meant this plague did not come so that Israel be sent free, but was a plague from heaven by the stars' arrangement over Egypt's fortune.

sources.quote: שאמרו אצבע אלהים היא, ולא אמרו אצבע ד' שהוא אלהי ישראל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the proof is that they said 'the finger of Elohim' and not 'the finger of the LORD', the God of Israel.

8:17.headline: 'The mixture': a jumble of beasts, or wolves of the evening?
8:17.body: Rashi says ערב is a mixture: all kinds of wild animals, snakes and scorpions together. Rashbam says it means wolves, named from ערב, evening, because they hunt at night, as in 'a wolf of the evenings'.

sources.quote: כָּל מִינֵי הַחַיּוֹת רָעוֹת וּנְחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים בְּעִרְבּוּבְיָא
sources.says: Rashi says it is all kinds of wild beasts, snakes and scorpions, mixed together.

sources.quote: אומר אני, כי מיני זאבים הם שנקראים ערוב, על שם שדרכם לטרוף בלילות, כדכתיב: (ירמיה ה, ו) זאב ערבות ישדדם
sources.says: Rashbam says kinds of wolves are called ערוב because they hunt at night, as it says 'a wolf of the evenings will ravage them' (Jeremiah 5:6).

8:19.headline: 'Redemption' here means a dividing line
8:19.body: פדות usually means redemption. Rashi says here it means a separation between God's people and Pharaoh's, and Rashbam says words for rescue all come from the idea of separating one thing from another.

sources.quote: ושמתי פדת. שֶׁיַּבְדִּיל בֵּין עַמִּי וּבֵין עַמְּךָ
sources.says: Rashi says it means God will separate between His people and Pharaoh's people.

sources.quote: ושמתי פדות - לשון הבדלה, וכן ישועה והצלה וחלצה פורקן, כולן לשון הפרשה והבדלה זה מזה
sources.says: Rashbam says פדות means separation, and so do salvation, rescue and release: all mean setting one thing apart from another.

sources.quote: ושמתי פדות. כטעם הפרש, וכל פדיון קרוב מזה הטעם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means a separation, and every kind of redemption is close to this sense.

8:22.headline: 'The abomination of Egypt': their god, or what they hate?
8:22.body: Rashi says תועבת מצרים means what Egypt worships, called an 'abomination' from Israel's side, as with 'the abomination of Ammon'. Or it means Israel's sacrifice is hateful to Egypt, because Israel would slaughter the very thing Egypt reveres.

sources.quote: תועבת מצרים. יִרְאַת מִצְרַיִם, כְּמוֹ "וּלְמִלְכֹּם תּוֹעֲבַת בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says it means the object of Egypt's worship, as in 'Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites'.

sources.quote: דָּבָר שָׂנאוּי הוּא לְמִצְרַיִם זְבִיחָה שֶׁאָנוּ זוֹבְחִים, שֶׁהֲרֵי יִרְאָתָם אָנוּ זוֹבְחִים
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: our sacrifice is hateful to the Egyptians, since we would be slaughtering what they revere.

8:27.headline: The wild animals left alive, so Egypt gained nothing from their hides
8:27.body: The frogs died, but here the wild animals are only 'removed'. Rashi says they did not die, because the Egyptians would then have profited from their skins.

sources.quote: ויסר הערב. וְלֹא מֵתוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁמֵּתוּ הַצְפַרְדְּעִים, שֶׁאִם מֵתוּ הָיָה לָהֶם הֲנָאָה בְּעוֹרוֹתָם
sources.says: Rashi says the beasts did not die as the frogs did, for if they had died the Egyptians would have benefited from their hides.

sources.quote: לא אמר וימת הערוב כמו שאמר בצפרדעים וימותו הצפרדעים, כי כוונת הש"י במכות הוא לצער אותם ולמרר את חייהם לא שיגיע להם מהם שום תועלת
sources.says: Bahya says the verse does not say the beasts died, as it did of the frogs, because God's aim in the plagues was to pain the Egyptians, not to let them gain anything.

9:3.headline: 'The hand of God': a way of speaking, not a body
9:3.body: Onkelos avoids the picture and renders 'a blow from before God'. Maimonides lists this very verse among the body words used of God, and says they all point to the acts such organs do, since 'the Torah speaks in human language'.

sources.quote: הָא מָחָא מִן קֳדָם יְיָ
sources.says: Onkelos renders: behold, a blow from before the Lord.

sources.quote: ואברי הביצוע המיוחסים לו: "יַד ה'" (שמות ט,ג)
sources.says: Maimonides lists 'the hand of God' in Exodus 9:3 among the organs of action attributed to God.

sources.quote: ושהם כולם נועדו להורות על פעולותיהם של אותם אברים
sources.says: He says all these body words are meant to point to the actions of those organs.

sources.quote: דברה תורה כלשון בני אדם
sources.says: He cites the rabbis: the Torah speaks in human language.

9:5.headline: A date set for the plague, so no one calls it natural
9:5.body: God fixed the next day for the cattle plague. Rashbam says the set time was so the Egyptians could not call it an ordinary plague of the land.

sources.quote: מועד לאמר - שלא יאמרו מכת מדינה היא
sources.says: Rashbam says the time was fixed so they would not say it was a common plague of the country.

9:8.headline: Piach: soot so fine the wind blows it away
9:8.body: Rashi says פיח comes from 'blowing': the wind puffs it up and makes it fly. Rashbam calls it fine ash that the wind lifts.

sources.quote: דָּבָר הַנִּפָּח מִן הַגֶּחָלִים עֲמוּמִים הַנִּשְׂרָפִים בַּכִּבְשָׁן
sources.says: Rashi says it is what blows off the smoldering coals burning in a kiln.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן הֲפָחָה, שֶׁהָרוּחַ מְפִיחָן וּמַפְרִיחָן
sources.says: Rashi says the word means blowing: the wind blows it and makes it fly.

sources.quote: פיח - אפר דק שמתנפח ברוח
sources.says: Rashbam says it is fine ash that is blown about by the wind.

9:10.headline: Boils on cattle, after all the cattle had died?
9:10.body: The cattle plague killed 'all the livestock of Egypt', so where did these animals come from? Rashi says the decree covered only animals in the field, while those who feared God's word had brought theirs inside; Ibn Ezra reads 'all' as 'most'.

sources.quote: מֵאַיִן הָיוּ לָהֶם הַבְּהֵמוֹת, וַהֲלֹא כְּבָר נֶאֱמַר וַיָּמָת כֹּל מִקְנֵה מִצְרָיִם
sources.says: Rashi asks where they had animals from, since it already said all the livestock of Egypt died.

sources.quote: לֹא נִגְזְרָה גְזֵרָה אֶלָּא עַל אוֹתָן שֶׁבַּשָּׂדוֹת בִּלְבַד
sources.says: Rashi answers that the decree was only on the animals in the fields.

sources.quote: ופי' וימת כל מקנה מצרים רובו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'all the livestock of Egypt died' means most of it.

9:14.headline: 'All My plagues': the hail, or the death of the firstborn?
9:14.body: Rashi learns from 'all My plagues' that the last plague, the death of the firstborn, weighed as much as all the others. Rashbam and Rabbeinu Bahya read it of the hail itself, which held many blows at once.

sources.quote: לָמַדְנוּ מִכָּאן שֶׁמַּכַּת בְּכוֹרוֹת שְׁקוּלָה כְּנֶגֶד כָּל הַמַּכּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says we learn from here that the plague of the firstborn equals all the plagues.

sources.quote: מגפתי - מיני חבלות והכאות: אש וברד
sources.says: Rashbam says 'my plagues' are the kinds of blows in the hail: fire and hail and more.

sources.quote: קרא למכת הברד כל מגפותי מפני שבמכת הברד נכללות מגפות הרבה
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the hail is called 'all My plagues' because it held many plagues within it.

9:18.headline: 'This time tomorrow': Moses marked the wall
9:18.body: Rashi says Moses scratched a line on the wall and told Pharaoh: tomorrow, when the sun reaches this mark, the hail will fall.

sources.quote: שָׂרַט לוֹ שְׂרִיטָה בַּכֹּתֶל – לְמָחָר כְּשֶׁתַּגִּיעַ חַמָּה לְכָאן, יֵרֵד הַבָּרָד
sources.says: Rashi says Moses scratched a mark on the wall: tomorrow when the sun reaches here, the hail will fall.

9:22.headline: 'Over the heavens': toward the sky, or above it?
9:22.body: Rashi gives the plain sense: stretch your hand toward the sky. He also brings a midrash that God lifted Moses up above the heavens.

sources.quote: לְצַד הַשָּׁמַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says it means toward the heavens.

sources.quote: וּמִדְרַשׁ אַגָּדָה: הִגְבִּיהוֹ הַקָּבָּ"ה לְמֹשֶׁה לְמַעְלָה מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם
sources.says: Rashi cites a midrash that God raised Moses above the heavens.

9:23.headline: Fire 'walked' to the ground: a borrowed verb
9:23.body: הלך is the verb for walking. Maimonides says it is borrowed for the spreading of things finer than living bodies, citing this fire; Ibn Ezra adds that fire going down to the earth goes against its nature, which is to rise.

sources.quote: מונח זה הושאל להתפשטות והימתחות של גופים שהם דקים יותר מגופי בעלי החיים
sources.says: Maimonides says the term is borrowed for the spreading of bodies finer than animal bodies.

sources.quote: וַתִּהֲלַךְ אֵשׁ אָרְצָה" (שמות ט,כג)
sources.says: He cites 'fire went down to the earth' as an example of that sense.

sources.quote: ארצה. הפך תולדתה כי היא למעלה עולה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says going down to earth is the opposite of fire's nature, which rises.

9:24.headline: Fire inside the hail: a miracle within a miracle
9:24.body: Hail is water, yet fire burned inside it. Rashi says the two made peace with each other to do their Creator's will; Ibn Ezra calls it a wonder within a wonder.

sources.quote: נֵס בְּתוֹךְ נֵס, הָאֵשׁ וְהַבָּרָד מְעֹרָבִין, וְהַבָּרָד מַיִם הוּא, וְלַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן קוֹנָם עָשׂוּ שָׁלוֹם בֵּינֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it was a miracle within a miracle: fire and hail mixed though hail is water, and to do their Maker's will they made peace.

sources.quote: ואש מתלקחת בתוךְ הברד. פלא בתוך פלא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra calls fire flaring inside hail a wonder within a wonder.

9:28.headline: Verav: 'enough already', or 'He has power to relieve'?
9:28.body: Rashi reads ורב as 'enough': what has fallen is plenty. Onkelos and Rabbeinu Bahya read it as 'great': God has ample power to bring relief.

sources.quote: ורב. דַּי לוֹ בְּמַה שֶּׁהוֹרִיד כְּבָר
sources.says: Rashi says: enough with what He has already sent down.

sources.quote: וְסַגִּי קֳדָמוֹהִי רְוַח
sources.says: Onkelos renders: and there is ample relief before Him.

sources.quote: ורב, להושיע הוא. וכן תרגם אונקלוס וסגי קדמוהי רווחא
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says it means He is great to save, as Onkelos renders.

9:29.headline: Why pray only once outside the city?
9:29.body: Rashi says Moses would not pray inside the city because it was full of idols. Ramban gives a plain reason: he wanted to spread his hands to the open sky and have the storm stop at once, which he could not do in town.

sources.quote: אֲבָל בְּתוֹךְ הָעִיר לֹא הִתְפַּלֵּל לְפִי שֶׁהָיְתָה מְלֵאָה גִּלּוּלִים
sources.says: Rashi says he did not pray inside the city because it was full of idols.

sources.quote: רָצָה לִהְיוֹת כַּפָּיו פְּרוּשׂוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְיַחְדְּלוּ הַקּוֹלוֹת וְהַמָּטָר מִיָּד, וְלֹא יִתָּכֵן לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן בָּעִיר
sources.says: Ramban says he wanted his hands spread toward the sky and the thunder and rain to stop at once, which could not be done in the city.

9:29.headline: 'The earth is the Lord's': His care reaches down here too
9:29.body: Ibn Ezra reads it simply: the land is God's, not Pharaoh's. Maimonides cites the verse against those who thought God's care stops at the moon and leaves the earth alone.

sources.quote: כי לד' הארץ. ולא לך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says: the earth is God's, and not yours.

sources.quote: שחשבו שהשגחתו יתעלה מסתיימת אצל גלגל הירח ואילו הארץ ואשר בה עזובים
sources.says: Maimonides rejects those who thought God's providence ends at the sphere of the moon and the earth is abandoned.

sources.quote: כלומר שהשגחתו גם בארץ כמתאים לה כמו שהוא משגיח בשמים כמתאים להם
sources.says: He says the verse means God watches over the earth as fits it, just as He watches over the heavens.

9:34.headline: 'He sinned again': now Pharaoh sins knowingly
9:34.body: Rashbam says that until now Pharaoh had not sinned on purpose. Once he had admitted 'I and my people are the wicked ones' and still went back, the Torah calls it sin.

sources.quote: עד עתה לא נתכוון לחטוא במזיד, אבל כשהודה על הברד: ואני ועמי הרשעים - לכן קוראו עכשיו מזיד
sources.says: Rashbam says until now he did not mean to sin deliberately, but after he admitted about the hail 'I and my people are wicked', it is called deliberate.

sources.quote: הרשעים כשיש להם צרה נכנעים וכשעברה מיד מתגאים
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the wicked bow when in trouble and turn proud as soon as it passes.
